attribution.note: Marcus's own words, listed as one of his three further predictions.

semantics.note: Firm 'will', so a scored forecast. 'Them' clearly means the AI industry from the previous line. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: Judging 'do little' over the administration's term is an ordinary plain reading. Ruling out early support and allowing early contradiction only on a major binding action is fair. 'Little' is vague, so the reading decides the result.

reviews.rationale: Open-ended forecast with no deadline. The packet has no evidence items, and no conclusive event, such as a major penalty or consent order against leading AI companies, is documented. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own commentary on The Information's CyberCartel report.

semantics.note: Two factual parts: hackers are increasing malicious agent use, and attacks do not require state-of-the-art frontier models. The 'disconcerting' framing is not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'state-of-the-art frontier' as the top-tier model fits Marcus's own context (existing models suffice even without future frontier models). Claude Opus and Sonnet are strong models, so the 'frontier' reading decides the second part.

evidence.note: Dated 2026-10-22. Reports CyberCartel sharply increased its use of AI agents in recent months.
Says attacks used models below Anthropic's top Mythos model, with fallback to smaller models such as Kimi. Supports the second part on the contract's reading.
Google GTIG Q3 2026 tracker: agents are automating more of attackers' work. Supports a broader 'stepping up' trend.
GTIG: adversaries use open-weight as well as commercial models to build working exploits. Supports 'don't need frontier'.
No fully autonomous pipelines seen in the wild yet. A nuance on how far agent use has gone; it does not contradict growth in agent use.

reviews.rationale: Both parts hold for mid-to-late 2026. CyberCartel and the GTIG tracker show growing malicious agent use. Damaging attacks used models below the top state of the art, with smaller-model fallbacks, and attackers used open-weight models for exploits. The second part depends on treating Opus and Sonnet as non-top-frontier, which the contract fairly does.

attribution.note: Marcus restates his own January 2025 Politico warning and reaffirms it with 'Well, here we are.'

semantics.note: Present-tense observation. 'Notoriously' becomes 'highly', which is close enough. 'No known solution' attaches mainly to prompt injection.

contract.note: Treating 'no known solution' as no generally accepted reliable fix, with partial mitigations not counting, is an ordinary reading. Testing it for 2026 matches the reaffirmation.

evidence.note: CSA summary of the May 2026 Five Eyes guidance: prompt injection is the most persistent, hard-to-fix threat, and defenses are immature.
Same summary: models cannot reliably separate instructions from content, and this remains unresolved at the model level.
June 2026 Infosecurity Europe: an OWASP contributor says prompt injection is unsolved at a fundamental level.
October 2026: CyberCartel bypassed commercial model guardrails with simple pretexts, showing jailbreaks still worked in practice.

reviews.rationale: Government guidance and expert testimony from 2026 say prompt injection has no fundamental fix, and a documented October 2026 case shows jailbreaks still worked. The packet notes a safety report on improved jailbreak resistance, but it was not provided as evidence, and in any case it does not show a reliable general defense.
